children: Short-dated British government bond yields rose to their highest level since 2023 on Wednesday after oil prices rose above $100 a barrel for the first time in six weeks, reviving inflation fears that pushed yields to their highest in decades last week.
Two-year gilt yields (GB2YT=RR), which are sensitive to interest expectations, reached 4.7172% at 1501 GMT, up more than 10 basis points on the day and their highest since November 2023.
Five-year yields (GB5YT=RR) peaked at 4.7967%, also up 10 bps and their highest since September 2023.

The moves worsen the financial arithmetic that will underpin finance minister John Healey's first budget next month, and follow the issuance of 30-year benchmark gilts on Tuesday that made for Britain's costliest borrowing since at least 1998.
"Whilst inflation and fiscal risks seem very well discounted at these levels, the risks are probably still skewed to the upside for yields," said Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK.
"That's particularly so for the UK where there is now a 7-week period of uncertainty ahead of the budget."
Long-dated gilts also had a bad day, underperforming against comparable German and U.S. debt, but not French.

The latest rise in energy prices prompted investors to increase bets on a Bank of England interest rate hike, with the OIS curve showing the chance of a quarter-point increase by November's meeting rising to 75% from 65% on Tuesday.

BoE Governor Andrew Bailey told a parliament committee on Tuesday that market pricing reflected the risk of further energy market pressure on inflation but that the BoE itself was not seeking to signal that a rate rise was coming.
